subtopic: Deciding whether to report a cheating friend
subtype: Approach: public shaming on social media [Pitfall]
passage: Ten p.m. before the science practical, and Wasim was still shaking with anger. Vaibhav had copied his lab report again, and the teacher had praised the neat diagram as Vaibhav's. Without thinking, Wasim typed into the class group: “Funny how some people's own work looks exactly like other people's homework.” He hit send and dropped the phone on the bed. By 10:20 there were twelve replies, all guessing. By 10:30 Vaibhav's name was in the chat, and someone had called him a cheat. By morning the rumour said Wasim had proof and had already reported him. Vaibhav met him at the gate: “You could have just told me.” The teacher, who had wanted a quiet word about the report, now had a shouting match in the corridor to deal with, and the practical started late.

qa.q: What did Wasim type into the class group?
qa.a: Wasim typed: Funny how some people's own work looks exactly like other people's homework.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he sent the message?
qa.a: Wasim was angry and, in the heat of it, wanted to hit back without thinking.

qa.q: What could Wasim do instead of posting?
qa.a: Wasim could speak to Vaibhav privately and, if it continued, tell the teacher, since copying is a matter for the teacher and not for the class group.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel on seeing his name in the group?
qa.a: Vaibhav would feel humiliated and angry, and his words You could have just told me show he was hurt at being shamed in public.

grounding: An angry teen posts a hint about the cheater in the class group, which humiliates the friend, spreads rumours and turns a matter for the teacher into a fight.
